flashcards.q: Why are factual grounding and brand voice conditioning treated as separate mechanisms in a production content pipeline?
flashcards.a: They're orthogonal properties of generated text controlled by different mechanisms -- a model can be perfectly on-brand in tone while stating a fabricated fact. RAG constrained to verified data handles grounding; fine-tuning/few-shot handles voice. Conflating them is a common naive-implementation mistake.

flashcards.q: What happened in the Air Canada chatbot case and what's the architectural lesson?
flashcards.a: The airline's support chatbot invented a bereavement-fare policy that didn't exist; a tribunal held Air Canada contractually bound by it, rejecting the 'separate legal entity' defense. Lesson: claims a customer could rely on (price, policy, availability) must be grounded in retrieved verified data with no open-generation path, not just disclaimed after the fact.

flashcards.q: Few-shot/prompt-based voice conditioning vs. fine-tuning -- tradeoffs?
flashcards.a: Few-shot: cheap, fast to iterate, weak under distribution shift/unusual inputs. Fine-tuning (typically LoRA/QLoRA): more robust and consistent at scale, slower/costlier to update, risks baking in errors present in the curated training corpus.

flashcards.q: What does a production quality gate score, and what's its job?
flashcards.a: A lightweight classifier (not another LLM call) scoring brand-voice adherence, factual-risk flags (price/date/superlative/health/financial claims), compliance flags, and fluency. Its job is TRIAGE -- routing by risk to auto-publish, spot-check, or mandatory human review -- not final judgment.

flashcards.q: How should a quality gate be calibrated, and what's commonly skipped?
flashcards.a: Against real downstream outcomes (precision/recall on published-vs-caught content), not just offline validation accuracy. Skipping this leads to either risky content slipping through or reviewers buried in false-positive flags.

flashcards.q: What is the rubber-stamping failure mode in human-in-the-loop review, and how do you detect it?
flashcards.a: When review volume exceeds capacity or the gate produces mostly false-positive flags, reviewers stop meaningfully scrutinizing content and approve by default -- 'human in the loop' becomes theater. Detect via secondary sampled independent review; a near-zero disagreement rate with high throughput signals rubber-stamping.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't an English-calibrated quality gate transfer to other locales?
flashcards.a: Hallucination rates, fluency, and what counts as on-brand tone vary by language/culture. Lower-resource languages typically show higher error rates due to less training representation, so an English-tuned threshold is usually too permissive elsewhere -- needs per-locale recalibration, not just prompt translation.

flashcards.q: Why is an audit trail (source fact to generated claim) treated as a compliance requirement in 2026?
flashcards.a: Given FTC enforcement priorities targeting deceptive AI marketing claims, EU AI Act content-labeling requirements, and legal precedent (Air Canada) holding companies liable for AI-generated claims, being able to show exactly which verified source grounded a published claim is the difference between a defensible and indefensible position if challenged.

flashcards.q: What content categories should almost never be fully automated with zero human review?
flashcards.a: Anything touching price commitments, availability guarantees, legal/regulatory claims, health/safety statements, or flagship brand messaging -- the cost of a single bad instance vastly outweighs the throughput cost of a human check.

flashcards.q: What FTC 2026 enforcement priorities are relevant to AI-generated marketing content?
flashcards.a: Deceptive AI marketing claims, AI systems overstating their own accuracy/objectivity/neutrality, and AI content not properly disclosed as AI-generated where that distinction affects consumer trust.

flashcards.q: Roughly how much cheaper is a budget-tier model than a frontier model for high-volume, low-risk content generation (early 2026 pricing)?
flashcards.a: Roughly 20-30x. Frontier models (GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6) run about $2.50-3/million input and ~$15/million output tokens; budget models (Gemini 1.5 Flash, GPT-4.1 Nano) run $0.075-0.10/$0.30-0.40 â€” making risk-tiered routing a cost lever, not just a quality one.

flashcards.q: By roughly how much does RAG-constrained generation reduce hallucination rates versus ungrounded generation, per published research?
flashcards.a: Roughly 30-70% across domains, with about a 40% aggregate improvement in factual accuracy; in structured-output tasks specifically, hallucinated fields drop from ~21% ungrounded to under 7.5% (steps) / under 4.5% (tables) with retrieval grounding.
